replies.text:
Permafrost does not prevent construction, it just makes it cost a bit more. Example, when building a road, we not to blast away all the permafrost we encounter with explosives and build a solid foundation for the road. Its like building a bridge over water. The foundation pillars are whats holding the road/bridge and they are anchored directly onto the bed rock beneath the permafrost. No matter how much the permafrost shifts, melts or reforms, it won't damage the road because the permafrost is not holding the road, its the pillars that are holding it. 
Canada is a lot more advanced then most think. Of course we don't build such roads everywhere, only the most important highways are built like that. For example, the railway upgrade that goes to Churchill is being built this way. 
Now as for farmland, Canada has a lot more then what is currently being farmed. Only the flat lands are being farmed as they are the easiest. But the Canadian Shield has the perfect conditions for farming too. It holds over 20% of the world's fresh water. There is over a million lakes in there. The soil is very fertile, but its small patches here and there. The land needs a lot of manual work. The soil needs to be gathered and terraces needs to be built to hold the soil in place so that farming on a large scale becomes possible. We could even have rice fields because fresh water that abondant. We just need to reshape the land into the shape of terraces. But almost no one wants to do it because Canada already produces too much food as it is.

comments.author: @SilverScarletSpider
comments.text:
Key Factors Explored: Russia people make less money per capita than Mexico and Poland
    Population Distribution & Climate: While both countries are cold, most Canadians live in a narrow, milder strip along the United States border (1:14-1:24). In contrast, millions of Russians live in much colder, inland regions across Siberia (1:33-2:17), which significantly increases infrastructure costs (4:40-4:53).
    Waterways & Trade: Canada benefits from the St. Lawrence waterway and Great Lakes system (6:45-7:15), which provide efficient, year-round access to global trade. Many of Russia's major rivers flow north into the frozen Arctic (5:10-5:40), and its major ports are often ice-bound or lack easy ocean access (6:05-6:35).
    Geopolitics: Russia has historically faced numerous invasions across its open plains, forcing the state to focus heavily on defense (8:01-8:50). Canada has enjoyed a stable, peaceful relationship with its only neighbor, the United States, allowing it to invest in growth rather than military fortification (9:15-10:07).
    Land Ownership & Economic History: Canada's Dominion Lands Act encouraged individual land ownership and investment (10:54-11:13). Russia’s history of serfdom and later Soviet collective farming prevented families from owning and improving their own property (10:13-10:50, 12:20-12:43), which created lasting economic disparities.
    Resource Dependence: While both countries are resource-rich, Russia is heavily dependent on oil and gas revenue to support its state budget (14:53-15:19). Canada has a more diversified, developed service and manufacturing economy, making it more resilient to fluctuations in global commodity prices (15:20-15:40).
